--- title: "[Graph.get_node_df()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method}" body-classes: doc-api-page doc-py-api-page shift-heading-level-by: 0 toc-depth: 3 page-navigation: false html-table-processing: none --- ::: {.doc-subject} Get nodes as a Polars DataFrame. ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/edgecase/blob/main/python/edgecase/graph.py#L13742-L13853){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-Kind.FUNCTION} ```python Graph.get_node_df() ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} ![Node DataFrame](/assets/graphs/get-node-df.light.svg){.lightbox fig-alt="The shared four-node graph A, B, C, D, each node tagged with its integer id 1 to 4. The result is a table with the columns id, label, type, and degree: one row per node sorted by id, type empty (null), and degrees 2, 3, 3, 2." width="100%"} Exports all nodes and their attributes to a Polars DataFrame for tabular analysis. Each row represents a node, with columns for the node ID and any attributes set on nodes. The DataFrame always includes 'id', 'label', and 'type' as the first three columns, sorted by `id` in ascending order. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [pl.DataFrame]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : A Polars DataFrame with mandatory columns 'id', 'label', 'type' (first three), followed by other attributes and 'degree'. Empty DataFrame if graph has no nodes. ::: ## Technical Notes {.doc-technical-notes} The column layout is deliberately stable so downstream code never has to guess: `id`, `label`, and `type` always come first (in that order), any custom node attributes follow in alphabetical order, and a computed `degree` column always closes the frame. Rows come sorted by `id` ascending. Missing values, whether an absent label, a node without the `type` attribute, or an attribute present on some nodes but not others, are represented as `None`, so Polars operations that respect nulls behave as expected. ## Examples {.doc-examples} Every node DataFrame starts with `id`, `label`, and `type`, followed by any custom attributes and a computed `degree` column: ::: {#171d9b9c .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec graph = ( ec.Graph() .add_nodes( [ ("A", {"type": "user", "score": 95}), ("B", {"type": "admin", "score": 88}), ("C", {"type": "user", "score": 92}), ] ) ) df = graph.get_node_df() df.columns ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` ['id', 'label', 'type', 'score', 'degree'] ``` ::: ::: ::: {#b8b8d67c .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} df.shape ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` (3, 5) ``` ::: ::: Since it's a regular Polars DataFrame, ordinary Polars operations work directly on it -- for example, averaging a numeric attribute: ::: {#d06c3c40 .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} df["score"].mean() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ``` 91.66666666666667 ``` ::: ::: Or counting how many nodes match a condition: ::: {#9646962a .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} import polars as pl df.filter(pl.col("type") == "user").height ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=4} ``` 2 ``` ::: ::: The computed `degree` column can be filtered on too, just like any other column: ::: {#871bdfc6 .cell execution_count=5} ``` {.python .cell-code} df.filter(pl.col("degree") > 5) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=5} ```{=html}
